title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
description: Given a binary search tree and two nodes `p` and `q` that both exist in it, return their **lowest common ancestor**: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants. A node counts as a descendant of itself. All values are unique.

examples.explanation: A node can be an ancestor of the other node.

constraints: p != q, and both exist in the tree
hints: Use the ordering property of a BST instead of searching the whole tree.
If both p and q are smaller than the current node, where must their common ancestor be? What if both are larger?
Walk down from the root: go left if both values are smaller, right if both are larger, otherwise the current node is the answer.

solution.explanation: Because of the BST ordering, compare p and q with the current node. If both are smaller, the answer is in the left subtree; if both are larger, it is in the right subtree; otherwise the paths to p and q split here (or one of them is this node), so this node is the answer. Walking down iteratively costs O(h) time and O(1) space.
